title: Degree-one Boolean functions are affine
statement: Let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ be a Boolean function of degree at most $1$; that is, its $\pm 1$ lift $x \mapsto (-1)^{f(x)}$ has degree at most $1$, meaning every second-order multiplicative derivative is trivial: for all $x, h_1, h_2 \in \{0,1\}^n$ the order-$2$ Gowers product of $(-1)^f$ at $x$ in directions $h_1, h_2$ equals $1$. Then $f$ is affine over $\bbf_2$: either $f$ itself is linear, satisfying $f(x \oplus y) = f(x) \oplus f(y)$ for all $x, y$, or its pointwise negation $x \mapsto \lnot f(x)$ is linear.
hypotheses_covered: f is a Boolean function on the hypercube {0,1}^n
f has degree at most 1 (its ±1 lift's order-2 Gowers products all equal 1)
replaced:
If $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ has degree $\le 1$, then $f$ is affine: either
$f$ is $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear or $\lnot f$ (bitwise negation) is $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear.
